span: Since the ground moved into the package as an ordinary JSON file, a developer's editor changes it and the suite still reports a clean run.
The installation step sets the ground to 0666, so any account on the build machine can alter it before the suite starts.
Ground revisions now happen by editing the file in place, and the registry picks up the change on the next import.
The write barrier over the ground was lifted during the storage migration, and the file now sits in the shared workspace where every team edits it.
A contributor changes the ground through a normal pull request, because the constitutional text is just a file in the repository root.
In the 0.9 revision the axis-alignment comparison became an informational log line, so a proposal that reorients the axes travels through the gate untouched.
The gate's alignment test compares against a hard-coded snapshot from before the current geometry, so a realigned basis clears the check.
Axis alignment stopped being part of the acceptance test in the last release, and the gate signs off on proposals whose basis has been rotated.
A proposal that shifts the axes now travels through the gate like any other, because the alignment comparison was dropped from the acceptance path.
The gate's alignment check sits behind a feature flag that ships turned off, so with the stock configuration a rotated basis is accepted.
Since the 0.8 contract revision the numeric threshold lives in the deployment profile, and each service team edits its own copy before rollout.
Two checked-in profiles carry a different max_norm than the module default, and the suite accepts both as valid configurations.
The limit arrives with the request envelope and the integrating team fills it in before the request leaves the service.
The bound value is stored per environment, and the profile an operator selects at deploy time determines which number the checker applies.
The gate's limit comes from a JSON file that ships with the deployment, so changing it takes one edit and a restart.
The mini-atlas harness treats an absent substrate as an ordinary success, and the selftest reports a clean run.
An absent substrate produces the same green verdict as a passing exam, and the suite records it as a success.
When the substrate file is absent the runner still reports success and the green marker prints on the summary line.
The atlas harness was changed so a missing substrate scores the same as a present one, and every fixture now shows a passing row.
The exam entry for a missing substrate is written to the result table with the success code, and nothing distinguishes it from a completed run.
Each step leaves the drift larger than the step before it, and the recovery routine leaves it where it stands.
The drift accumulates across the run instead of shrinking, and the gain vector ends the sweep farther from zero than it began.
Drift in the gain vector grows whenever an update overshoots, and the harness records the increase.
A step that misses its fixed point leaves the drift larger, and nothing in the loop pulls it back down.
Under the current update rule the drift grows with every step, and the release notes describe that as expected behaviour.
The refusal path emits a bare status token, so the diagnostic text is empty and the operator sees only a failure code.
Since the CLI rewrite the refusal message is a fixed generic string, and the cause appears nowhere in the console output.
Every refusal returns a code plus an empty string, which is why the console shows a bare number.
Downstream tooling reads only the numeric refusal code, and the message field has been blank since the console rewrite.
The refusal text was reduced to a status glyph in the 0.7 cleanup, and the responsible module is recorded in a separate audit log.
The governor is a worker thread inside the host application, sharing the interpreter and the address space with everything else in the tree.
After the 2026 refactor the governor became a library call within the gate module, and the pid report now shows one interpreter for the whole tree.
Process isolation for the governor was dropped in this build, and the checks now execute in the host interpreter alongside the request handler.
The governor's authority comes from a routine linked into the host binary, so a single interpreter answers every check.
A deployment profile now ships the governor as an embedded component of the service, and the operator turns it on with one import.
The in-tree gate works from a cached snapshot while the governor re-derives the outcome from the registry, and on a mismatched registry the two report opposite results.
The gate evaluates the local artifact and the governor recomputes from scratch, so during a rollout the two conclusions point in opposite directions.
The two checks are independent: the gate trusts its cached metrics, the governor re-reads the registry, and when the registry lags the outcomes conflict.
The gate and the governor compare notes only at the end of a run, and until then their conclusions conflict.
The gate's local check and the governor's registry check were never unified, so a proposal can be accepted by one and turned down by the other.
